title: Human response: Stronger assistance can reduce effort
desc: Uses formal models to show verification and behavioural adjustment condition joint performance, rather than empirically proving productivity effects.

kps.k: AI assistance changes human effort and decisions, so stronger assistance does not guarantee higher productivity.
kps.d: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes models effort as a choice rather than a fixed input. With concave production and linear effort costs, optimal effort weakly decreases as skill or assistance rises. A separate conditional comparison shows that lower effort can coexist with higher production. The substantive distinction is between substituting for human effort and reducing output: the former does not establish the latter.

kps.k: Contrasting productivity predictions reflect different model assumptions, not an empirical disagreement.
kps.d: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes derives opposite effects of increasing assistance under different production-curvature conditions. With concave production and convex effort costs, its IARA case additionally requires Condition D.4 and sufficiently large assistance for productivity to decline; its DARA case yields increasing productivity. These proofs identify conditions under which gains can reverse, rather than establishing that better AI generally helps or harms performance.

kps.k: Verification accuracy and signal use condition the benefits of combining human expertise with AI.
kps.d: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes shows that constant verification accuracy of at least one-half preserves decreasing expected effort in skill under concave production and linear costs. Skill-dependent verification can instead produce non-monotonic effort in certain parameter cases. The supplied radiology proof separately constructs cases where combined-signal decisions differ from human-only decisions and gives a conditional value comparison favouring human-only decisions, with equality when specified actions coincide. Neither result establishes that human oversight or combined decision-making universally improves performance.

kps.k: The practical implication is to test behavioural responses and joint performance rather than infer gains from AI capability alone.
kps.d: The AI models motivate measuring output separately from effort and examining how skill, checking accuracy and decision rules affect assisted work. This is an implication of the theory, not a tested deployment recommendation. All supplied material consists of proof fragments; even the radiology excerpts provide no experimental estimates. Missing definitions, damaged notation and truncated conclusions prevent reconstructing some thresholds and limiting results. The cluster therefore supplies conditional mechanisms and hypotheses, not effect sizes or evidence of outcomes in legal practice.

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition chiefly by treating human response and joint human–AI performance as conditional mechanisms rather than settled empirical effects. The most directly relevant model shows that stronger assistance can reduce optimal human effort, while lower effort need not mean lower output; it also derives opposite productivity effects under different production-curvature and cost assumptions. The radiology proof similarly shows that human-only and combined-signal decisions and values can diverge under specified conditions, without establishing a universal advantage for either approach. Material internal variation concerns relevance rather than substantive opposition: the credence-goods paper reinforces the synthesis’s methodological caution by supplying only formal monotonicity and derivative restrictions, while the incomplete-contracts paper addresses equilibrium price bounds and does not provide enough evidence to determine a position on AI assistance. Thus, this curated set supports testing effort, verification and joint outcomes separately, but it does not supply effect sizes or empirical proof of productivity consequences.

elens.an: The sole supplied pre-2015 source neither supports nor challenges the principal proposition that stronger AI assistance can reduce human effort and that verification and behavioural adjustment condition joint performance. Its contribution is a formal incomplete-contracts analysis: equilibrium incentive constraints are used to derive lower and upper bounds on expected-price differences by averaging across permutations. This is consistent with the cluster’s broader methodological emphasis on conditional mathematical results, but it provides no account of AI assistance, endogenous human effort, verification, or productivity. Its variables therefore cannot be translated into claims about human–AI performance. Because this curated time-period evidence contains only this source, material internal variation within the period cannot be assessed.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition’s cautious methodological core: the supplied materials establish conditional mathematical relationships rather than empirical productivity effects, so they do not justify inferring gains from stronger AI capability alone. The radiology source is the more direct support because it formally allows human-only and combined-signal decisions—and their values—to differ depending on specified conditions, reinforcing the importance of verification, decision rules and joint performance. The credence-goods source supports the proposition only indirectly: it proves monotonicity and derivative restrictions in an equilibrium model but supplies no basis for interpreting those variables as AI assistance, human effort or productivity. Thus, there is material variation in relevance, but not opposition: one source addresses conditional human–AI decision performance, while the other mainly reinforces the synthesis’s warning against translating formal results into organisational outcomes. Because these are proof fragments, not reported experimental estimates, neither establishes effect sizes or a general productivity advantage or disadvantage.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by formally modelling human effort as endogenous: under concave production and linear effort costs, stronger assistance can weakly reduce optimal effort, while a separate comparison shows that lower effort can coexist with higher production. It also supports the synthesis’s central qualification that AI capability alone does not determine joint productivity. Material internal variation comes from the model’s assumptions: productivity decreases with sufficiently strong assistance under the specified IARA and Condition D.4 case, but increases under DARA with convex effort costs; constant verification accuracy preserves decreasing expected effort in skill and q, whereas skill-dependent verification can make the skill-effort relationship non-monotonic. These are conditional mathematical predictions rather than empirical effect estimates, and damaged or truncated proof fragments limit reconstruction of some parameter restrictions.
